q: What is the standard time window for mechanical thrombectomy in anterior circulation stroke?
o: Within 6 hours (up to 24 hours in selected patients)
why: Thrombectomy is within 6 hours, extended to 24 hours if imaging shows a small core with a large salvageable area (DAWN). Thrombolysis is within 4.5 hours.

q: What systolic BP target is used during thrombectomy before reperfusion?
why: Systolic 140–180 mmHg (within about 10% of baseline) protects the penumbra; also normoxia, normocapnia, normothermia and glucose 7.8–10 mmol/L.

q: Which factor favours GA over conscious sedation for thrombectomy?
o: Anterior circulation stroke in a calm patient
why: GA is favoured for agitation, hiccups, vomiting, posterior circulation strokes, complex anatomy or dominant hemisphere involvement.

q: During thrombectomy under GA, the EtCO2 is 3.2 kPa. Why is this a problem?
o: Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction, reducing perfusion to the penumbra
why: Avoid hyperventilation: hypocapnia constricts cerebral vessels and worsens ischaemia. Aim for normocapnia.

q: What proportion of strokes are ischaemic?

o: The dead core of the infarct
Potentially salvageable tissue around the infarct core
why: The penumbra can recover if perfusion is restored quickly ("time is brain").

q: Which trial supported thrombectomy as first-line treatment for anterior circulation large vessel occlusion?
why: MR CLEAN supported endovascular thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion.

q: A patient becomes hypotensive and hypoxic after a groin puncture for thrombectomy with a rising heart rate. Which procedural complication should be considered?
why: Femoral access can cause retroperitoneal haemorrhage; other complications include vessel dissection and subarachnoid haemorrhage.

q: In the neurointerventional suite, what heparin dose is typically given?
why: Neurointerventional procedures use 70–100 u/kg heparin targeting ACT 2–3× baseline.
